metadata.note: The New York Central's Hudson Division, New York-Albany, the southern leg shared by nearly every Amtrak train out of New York's Empire Corridor. GEOMETRY CORRECTED 2026-08-24: the route was previously the 58-point GTFS-derived Amtrak shape (median vertex spacing 3.4 km), whose last 10 km into Albany were two straight chords across the river bends, and which stopped on the EAST bank at Rensselaer for every era including those when trains ran into Albany itself. It is now real-traced from OpenStreetMap, and the Albany approach is drawn properly: north past Rensselaer, west over the Livingston Avenue Bridge, then south down the west bank. The 1851-1866 era is split out as its own feature ending at East Albany, because before the bridge opened there was no rail crossing and passengers took a ferry. headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era remain estimates, not from real timetables.
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_River_Railroad and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Central_Railroad (Hudson River Railroad completed New York-Albany Oct 1851; Vanderbilt merged the Hudson River, Harlem and New York Central in 1869; Grand Central Terminal opened 1913)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livingston_Avenue_Bridge and https://www.newyorkalmanack.com/2025/09/albany-livingston-railroad-bridge/ (first engine over the bridge Feb 18 1866, passenger trains from Feb 22; before it, trains from the east terminated opposite Albany and passengers crossed by ferry)
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Headways and speeds are estimates throughout, from no timetable. The drawn line is the corridor as it survives today, so any 19th-century realignment is not reflected -- notably the exact Albany-side approach and terminal trackage, and the East Albany terminal and ferry slip of the 1851-1866 era, which are not drawn. The 1866 split is dated to the bridge opening, which is sourced, but the date the last ferry ran is not.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.line: Hudson River: New York – East Albany (Greenbush)
properties.speed_source: estimated: 1850s-60s express service on a new water-level line; unsourced

segments.note: The Hudson River Railroad completed its New York-Albany line up the east bank in Oct 1851 (see metro_north.geojson for the commuter-served southern end of the same line). IT DID NOT REACH ALBANY: there was no bridge, so trains terminated at East Albany, opposite the city, and passengers crossed by ferry. That is why this feature stops on the east bank. Frequency estimated/unsourced
sources: NOT SOURCED AT SEGMENT LEVEL: the references below cover this line, but nothing has been checked specifically against this segment's start year, end year or service. Treat the dates and the headway as unverified. Supporting references for the line:

properties.geometry_source: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap (ODbL) via Overpass: railway ways along the east-bank corridor, filtered to the corridor and shortest-pathed from Grand Central to Rensselaer, then a second trace from Rensselaer over the Livingston Avenue Bridge and back down the west bank to the Albany Union Station site. REPLACES the previous geometry, which was the 58-point GTFS-derived Amtrak shape copied from amtrak.geojson -- median vertex spacing 3.4 km, with the last 10 km into Albany drawn as two straight chords cutting across the river bends.
properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced, 2791 points, median vertex spacing 54 m, 90th percentile 176 m; only 2 steps of the main line exceed 1 km. No leg is a straight-line placeholder. Traced 141.2 mi against the 139.9 mi of the superseded sketch; no company mileage has been checked. LATER ALIGNMENT: this is the corridor as it survives today (CSX Hudson Subdivision / Amtrak Empire Corridor), not a verified 19th-century alignment. Terminates on the east bank at Rensselaer, which is correct for this era -- there was no Hudson bridge at Albany before 1866.

properties.line: Hudson River: New York – Albany (via the Livingston Avenue Bridge)

segments.note: The Livingston Avenue Bridge opened in 1866 -- first engine across Feb 18, passenger trains from Feb 22 -- and trains could finally run into Albany itself. The approach is not a straight run into the city: the line continues north up the east bank past Rensselaer, crosses the bridge above the city, and comes back south down the west bank to the Albany Union Station site. Frequency estimated/unsourced
